title: Bagging & random forests: stronger than the sum of trees
intro: Against high variance: ensembles. Bagging trains dozens of deep trees each on a different bootstrap sample and averages; random forests let each split see only a random handful of features. With OOB scores and the variance formula that explains it all.
keyPoints: A deep tree has low bias but high variance. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains B trees on B different bootstrap sets and averages the predictions: same bias, far less variance.

A bootstrap set is n draws with replacement from your n training samples: on average 63.2% unique and 36.8% duplicates — and exactly those unused samples give each tree a free validation set (the OOB score).

Random forests decorrelate the trees: at each split the tree chooses from only m of the p features (m = √p for classification). Ensemble variance is ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — a smaller correlation ρ lowers the plateau that B trees converge to.

More trees cannot overfit: variance drops monotonically towards the plateau ρσ² and stays there. n_estimators = 100–200 is almost always enough; tune max_features, max_depth and min_samples_leaf instead.
The OOB score evaluates each tree on its own 36.8% unseen samples — a free, nearly k-fold-equivalent estimate without a single extra fit.

sections.title: Why one tree is not enough

blocks.html: A fully grown tree is unbeatable on training data, but its structure is shaky: swap a handful of samples and the root split, thresholds and leaves can all change. That is high variance in the flesh.

The classic fix for a jittery estimator: measure repeatedly and average. Train a hundred different trees on a hundred versions of your data and their shared errors cancel out — the trees may be deep and unruly for exactly that reason.

Bagging replaces one stubborn learner with a committee of a hundred, each trained slightly differently — and the committee decides. Regression: average; classification: majority vote or averaged probability.

sections.title: Bootstrap: new data from your own data

blocks.html: The bootstrap: draw n samples with replacement. Each set has exactly n rows but a different mix: roughly two thirds of the original samples appear, one third is missing.

blocks.label: Probability one sample is NOT in the bootstrap set
blocks.caption: Each draw misses a given sample with probability 1 − 1/n, and there are n draws. For large n that approaches 36.8% — so on average 63.2% of the samples are (at least once) in the set.

blocks.html: At n = 100, \( (1 - 0.01)^{100} = 0.366 \): on average 63.2% unique per set. Those 36.8% missing samples are a gift: use them as a mini test set for exactly that tree — that is the out-of-bag score (OOB).

blocks.caption: see the 63.2% with your own eyes
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100

for b in range(1, 4):
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=n)   # n draws with replacement
    uniek = len(np.unique(idx))
    print(f'bootstrap set {b}: {uniek}% unique samples')

print(f'theory: {(1 - 1/n)**n:.1%} of samples missing on average')

blocks.html: Typical output: three sets with 62–64% unique samples, and the theory rule predicting 36.6%.
Why with replacement? The set stays as large as the training data and the multiplicities add extra variety — a sample appearing three times weighs three times as heavily in that one tree.

The recipe: (1) B bootstrap sets, (2) per set a fully grown, unregularized tree (no max_depth — you want low bias per tree), (3) aggregate: mean (regression) or majority vote (classification). In scikit-learn: BaggingClassifier/BaggingRegressor.

blocks.label: Ensemble prediction (regression)
blocks.caption: f_b is the tree trained on bootstrap set b. For classification: vote (hard voting) or average probabilities (soft voting) — soft is usually slightly better.

blocks.html: Why averaging works: with independent errors the variance of the mean drops to \( \sigma^2/B \) — 100 trees = 100× less noise. It never gets that far (trees share the same data, so their errors correlate at \( \rho \)), but the direction holds: bias stays, variance drops.
The OOB score: for every sample, only the trees that never saw it (~36.8%) predict, aggregated and compared to the true label — a test-score estimate without touching the test set.
Practical: set oob_score=True and treat model.oob_score_ as your first sanity check. If OOB is poor while train is perfect, the forest still overfits.

Bagging has one blind spot: if one feature is overwhelmingly predictive, nearly every tree picks it at the root and the trees grow alike — high correlation \( \rho \), high plateau. Random forests break that dominance at the split itself.

The intervention: at every split the algorithm draws a random m of the p features and the tree may choose only from those. Defaults: \( m = \sqrt{p} \) (classification) or \( p/3 \) (regression). Each tree gets slightly worse — but the trees become fundamentally different.

blocks.label: ENSEMBLE VARIANCE
blocks.caption: σ² is the per-tree variance, ρ the average pairwise correlation between trees, B the number of trees. Derived for the mean of B equally distributed, pairwise correlated estimators.

blocks.html: Read the formula term by term: the second term \( \sigma^2/B \) shrinks away with more trees; the first term \( \rho\sigma^2 \) is the plateau and depends only on \( \rho \). More trees always helps, but vanishes into the fog if \( \rho \) stays high — random forests are precisely the knob on \( \rho \).

blocks.title: The plateau of ensemble variance
blocks.subtitle: Horizontal: the number of trees B; vertical: the variance of the ensemble. The cyan curve follows your sliders for ρ and σ²; green is the dream (ρ = 0: variance shrinks without a floor), magenta the nightmare (ρ = 1: all trees identical — zero benefit). Drag ρ down and watch the plateau sink: exactly what feature subsampling does. The yellow dot is your current ensemble.

blocks.html: At the start values variance sits at 0.296; drag B to 100 and almost nothing happens (0.246 — the plateau). Drag \( \rho \) to 0.1 and the plateau drops to 0.08: an order of magnitude no number of trees could ever buy.

Stubborn myth: “too many trees causes overfitting”. No — more trees cannot hurt generalization; they only cost compute and prediction time. A forest can overfit via trees that are too deep — but that knob is max_depth, not n_estimators.

sections.title: Hyperparameters: what to tune (and what to leave alone)

blocks.html: A random forest needs surprisingly little attention — hence its reputation as a “strong default”. The table is the honest priority list:

rows: number of trees — averages variance out, plateau stays
candidate features per split — THE correlation knob ρ
top priority: try √p, p/3 or log₂ p
brake on individual trees — bias up, even less variance
minimum samples per leaf — gentler brake than depth
turns on the free generalisation estimate
how many CPU cores train in parallel (−1 = all)
always −1 locally, no effect on the model

blocks.html: Tuning order: fix oob_score=True and n_estimators=100, scan max_features (√p, half, all p), and only then touch the tree brakes. Rarely needed.
Do not skip the scaling step once the forest is combined in a pipeline with other models or preprocessing — keep that pipeline identical across candidates.

sections.title: Feature importance: what do the trees care about?

blocks.html: The mean decrease in impurity (MDI, what feature_importances_ returns) sums per feature how much weighted impurity dropped and totals 1: 0.17 = “responsible for 17% of all purity gain”.
Take it with salt: MDI is biased toward features with many possible thresholds (IDs, timestamps). More robust: permutation importance — shuffle one feature and watch how much the score drops.
Two features carrying the same signal share importance; a feature can score low yet matter in interaction. Use importance for exploration, not as proof.

sections.title: In code: from one tree to a forest

blocks.html: Same breast cancer split, three models side by side: the unbridled tree, plain bagging and the full random forest — with OOB scores.

blocks.caption: tree vs. bagging vs. random forest (with OOB)
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, BaggingClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                          random_state=42)

models = {
    '1 tree':            DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
    'bagging (100)':     BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
                                           n_estimators=100, oob_score=True,
                                           random_state=42),
    'random forest (100)': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,
                                                  oob_score=True,
                                                  random_state=42),
}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    oob = f'{m.oob_score_:.3f}' if hasattr(m, 'oob_score_') else '  —'
    print(f'{name:22s} test-score={m.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}   oob={oob}')

blocks.html: Typical output: single tree 0.951; bagging 0.958 (OOB 0.955); random forest 0.965 (OOB 0.960). Both ensembles beat the tree, the forest beats bagging, and OOB tracks within half a point.

blocks.caption: feature importance of the forest
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

data = load_breast_cancer()
forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
forest.fit(data.data, data.target)

imp = forest.feature_importances_
order = np.argsort(imp)[::-1]
print('top-5 most important features:')
for i in order[:5]:
    print(f'  {data.feature_names[i]:25s} {imp[i]:.3f}')
print(f'  sum over all 30 features: {imp.sum():.1f}')

blocks.html: Typical output: worst concave points leads with 0.172, followed by worst area (0.123) and mean concave points (0.090); the sum across all 30 features is exactly 1.0.
Random forests are one end of the ensemble spectrum: parallel, variance hunter. The other end is boosting: trees in sequence repairing each other's errors — a bias hunter.
